DIOPTRA / HERO OF ALEXANDRIA, CHAPTER 31

Water needs
a clock.

Equal sections can deliver unequal supplies. A short observation can misrepresent a changing flow.

Reopen these settings. This file embeds its diagrams, full chapter reading, four printed pages, fonts and licenses. It makes no external subresource requests.

The collection experiment

Both wetted sections are 12 × 4 cm, area 48 cm². A travels at 10 cm/s. B travels at 30 cm/s for the first ten seconds, then 10 cm/s. The saved frame is 20 s.

A modern ideal experiment: centimetres, seconds, litres, uniform section-mean speeds and the twenty-second schedule are chosen. All outflow is collected without leakage or storage delay. These are not measurements of an ancient spring or a conversion of Hero’s fingers and sundial hours.

For the uniform mean speeds used here, supply = wetted area × mean speed. A litre is 1,000 cm³. The modern equation explains the experiment; the chapter gives no algebraic discharge formula.

Measure an interval

Blue: A. Green: B. Dashed ochre: B’s selected average extended from an empty receiver to twenty seconds. Shading marks the measured window; the dotted vertical line marks the saved replay frame.

Selected interval: 0–20 s. Volume divided by elapsed time gives an interval average.
StreamStart / LEnd / LCollected / LAverage / L/s
A09.69.60.48
B019.219.20.96

The selected B average is 19.2 L ÷ 20 s = 0.96 L/s. Applied to the whole twenty seconds, it predicts 19.2 L. The complete record contains 19.2 L. Difference: 0 L.

A short interval measures its own average. Extending it requires the flow to remain representative. The whole record’s average remains valid even when the instantaneous speed changes. At the exact ten-second switch, the displayed current speed is the speed after the change; cumulative volume remains continuous.

Read the complete chapter

Eleven units from Schöne’s edited chapter 31; Greek adapted from the Harvard College Library / Open Greek and Latin transcription, with a new English translation and language notes. Greek and new teaching text: CC BY-SA 4.0. The 1903 German translation is retained in the facing scans.

Dioptra 31 · p. 284, lines 11–12

1. Investigate a spring

Πηγῆς ὑπαρχούσης ἐπισκέψασθαι τὴν ἀπόρρυσιν αὐτῆς, τουτέστι τὴν ἀνάβλυσιν, ὅση ἐστίν.

Given a spring, to investigate its outflow—that is, how much it wells up.

πηγῆς ὑπαρχούσης · a spring being present

A genitive absolute supplies the starting condition. The aorist infinitive ἐπισκέψασθαι states the task: ‘to investigate’. It does not say the investigation took place in the past.

Dioptra 31 · p. 284, lines 12–13

2. The supply does not stay the same

εἰδέναι μέντοι χρὴ ὅτι οὐκ ἀεὶ ἡ ἀνάβλυσις ἡ αὐτὴ διαμένει.

One must, however, know that the flow does not always remain the same.

οὐκ ἀεὶ … ἡ αὐτή · not always … the same

Χρή with an infinitive expresses necessity: ‘one must know’. The article in ἡ αὐτή makes αὐτή mean ‘the same’. This opening matters when a short observation is extended to a longer period.

Dioptra 31 · p. 284, lines 14–18

3. Rain and drought

ὄμβρων μὲν γὰρ ὄντων ἐπιτείνεται διὰ τὸ ἐπὶ τῶν ὀρῶν τὸ ὕδωρ πλεονάζον βιαιότερον ἐκθλίβεσθαι, αὐχμῶν δὲ ὄντων ἀπολήγει ἡ ῥύσις διὰ τὸ μὴ ἐπιφέρεσθαι πλέον ὕδωρ. αἱ μέντοι γενναῖαι πηγαὶ οὐ παρὰ πολὺ τὴν ἀνάβλυσιν ἴσχουσιν.

For when there are rains it increases, because the abundant water on the mountains is forced out more strongly; but when there are droughts the flow falls away, because no more water is brought in. Strong springs, however, vary their flow only a little.

ὄμβρων μὲν … αὐχμῶν δέ · when there are rains … but when there are droughts

Two genitive absolutes balance rain against drought with μέν … δέ. Διὰ τὸ plus an infinitive gives a reason. The edition’s apparatus records corrections in the rain sentence; this reading follows the printed text. The experiment’s abrupt ten-second switch is a teaching device, not a model of rainfall response.

Dioptra 31 · p. 284, lines 18–21

4. Capture all the water

δεῖ οὖν περιλαβόντα τὸ πᾶν τῆς πηγῆς ὕδωρ, ὥστε μηδαμόθεν ἀπορρεῖν, σωλῆνα τετράγωνον μολιβοῦν ποιῆσαι, στοχασάμενον μᾶλλον μείζονα πολλῷ τῆς ἀποθύσεως·

One must therefore enclose all the spring’s water, so that none flows away elsewhere, and make a square lead pipe, judging it to be considerably larger than the discharge requires.

τὸ πᾶν … ὕδωρ · all the water

Πᾶν agrees with the neuter ὕδωρ. The instruction is about complete capture: a receiver that misses some of the water understates the supply. The pipe is square; the water need not fill its opening. The model uses an ideal rectangular stream and complete collection.

Dioptra 31 · pp. 284, line 21 – 286, line 1

5. Use the dioptra to find the low outlet

εἶτα δι’ ἑνὸς τόπου ἐναρμόσαι αὐτὸν ὥστε δι’ αὐτοῦ τὸ ἐν τῇ πηγῇ ὕδωρ ἀπορρεῖν. δεῖ δὲ αὐτὸν κεῖσθαι εἰς τὸν ταπεινότερον τῆς πηγῆς τόπον, ὥστε ἔχειν αὐτὴν ἀπόρρυσιν· τὸν δὲ ταπεινότερον ἐπιγνωσόμεθα τῆς πηγῆς τόπον διὰ τῆς διόπτρας.

Then fit it through one place so that the water in the spring flows out through it. It must lie at the spring’s lower place, so that the spring has an outlet; we shall identify the spring’s lower place by means of the dioptra.

διὰ τῆς διόπτρας · by means of the dioptra

Διά with the genitive names the means. Ταπεινότερον is comparative: ‘lower’. Here the surveying instrument chooses a place for the outlet; the later sundial supplies time. They do different jobs.

Dioptra 31 · p. 286, lines 1–6

6. Six times two makes twelve

ἀπολήψεται οὖν τὸ ἀπορέον διὰ τοῦ σωλῆνος ὕδωρ ἐν τῷ περιστομίῳ τοῦ σωλῆνος· οἷον ἀπολαμβάνει δακτύλους β· ἐχέτω δὲ καὶ τὸ πλάτος τοῦ περιστομίου τοῦ σωλῆνος δακτύλους ϛ· ἑξάκις δύο γίνονται ιβ· ⟨ἀποφανούμεθα δὴ τὴν ἀνάβλυσιν τῆς πηγῆς δακτύλων ιβ⟩.

The water flowing through the pipe will occupy part of its mouth: for example, it occupies two finger-widths in depth; let the mouth’s width also be six finger-widths. Six times two makes twelve. ⟨We shall then declare the spring’s flow to be twelve fingers.⟩

ἑξάκις δύο · six times two

Β = 2, ϛ = 6, ιβ = 12. ‘In depth’ makes explicit the dimension paired with width, as Schöne’s German does. The product measures a cross-sectional area even though the text says ‘fingers’. It is not a volume per time. Angle brackets preserve the editor’s relocated conclusion; the final duplicate is deleted in the printed edition.

Dioptra 31 · p. 286, lines 6–9

7. Size is insufficient

εἰδέναι δὲ χρὴ ὅτι οὐκ ἔστιν αὔταρκες πρὸς τὸ ἐπιγνῶναι, πόσον χορηγεῖ ὕδωρ ἡ πηγή, τὸ εὑρεῖν τὸν ὄγκον τοῦ ῥεύματος, ὃν λέγομεν εἶναι δακτύλων ιβ,

But one must know that finding the size of the stream, which we call twelve fingers, is not sufficient to discover how much water the spring supplies;

οὐκ ἔστιν αὔταρκες · it is not sufficient

The subject is the articular infinitive τὸ εὑρεῖν, ‘finding’. Ὄγκος is rendered ‘size’ here, not automatically modern three-dimensional ‘volume’: the preceding two lengths produced an area. This sentence continues into the next unit.

Dioptra 31 · p. 286, lines 9–11

8. The missing quantity is speed

ἀλλὰ καὶ τὸ τάχος αὐτοῦ· ταχυτέρας μὲν γὰρ οὔσης τῆς ῥύσεως πλέον ἐπιχορηγεῖ τὸ ὕδωρ, βραδυτέρας δὲ μεῖον.

its speed is needed too. For when the flow is faster it supplies more water; when slower, less.

τάχος / πάχος · speed / thickness

The edited text reads τάχος, ‘speed’; Schöne’s apparatus at lines 9–10 records τὸ πάχος, ‘thickness’. A single letter changes the quantity. This lesson follows the edited reading and the following faster/slower comparison; it does not present that choice as an autograph we can inspect. Ταχυτέρας and βραδυτέρας are feminine comparatives agreeing with ῥύσεως.

Dioptra 31 · p. 286, lines 11–14

9. Collect the water and observe the time

διὸ δεῖ ὑπὸ τὴν τῆς πηγῆς ῥύσιν ὀρύξαντα τάφρον τηρῆσαι ἐξ ἡλιακοῦ ὡροσκοπίου, ἐν τινὶ ὥρᾳ πόσον ἀπορρεῖ ὕδωρ ἐν τῇ τάφρῳ,

Therefore one must dig a trench beneath the spring’s outflow and observe by a sundial how much water flows into the trench in a certain interval;

ἐξ ἡλιακοῦ ὡροσκοπίου · by a solar time indicator

Ἡλιακοῦ describes the instrument as solar: a sundial. Τάφρος is a trench or ditch used here to receive the water. The text supplies no numerical timing interval or receiver dimensions. Our graduated vessels and modern seconds make the method visible; they are not a reconstruction of that equipment.

Dioptra 31 · p. 286, lines 14–15

10. Estimate a longer supply

καὶ οὕτως στοχάσασθαι τὸ ἐπιχορηγούμενον ὕδωρ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ πόσον ἐστίν,

and in this way estimate how much water is supplied in the day,

στοχάσασθαι · to estimate

An aorist middle infinitive continues δεῖ, ‘one must’. The wording calls for an estimate. Applying a short sample’s rate to a longer period requires the sample to represent that period. The changing-flow exercise exposes that assumption; it does not convert an ancient hour into a fixed number of seconds.

Dioptra 31 · p. 286, lines 15–17

11. The opening need not be measured

ὥστ’ οὐδὲ ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι τὸν ὄγκον τῆς ῥύσεως τηρεῖν· διὰ γὰρ τοῦ χρόνου δήλη ἐστὶν ἡ χορηγία.

so that it is not even necessary to observe the size of the flowing stream: through the time, the supply becomes clear.

διὰ τοῦ χρόνου · through the time

The article and genitive follow διά. The conclusion depends on the preceding collection of water as well as the time observation. Time alone cannot determine a volume. Measuring collected volume over an interval bypasses a separate measurement of the opening and speed.

What the evidence does and does not say

The source example multiplies two finger-widths by six. It then calls the result twelve fingers. The product is a section, not a supply per time. No fixed finger-to-centimetre conversion is used here. The source names a sundial and an interval, without a numerical duration; our modern seconds do not reconstruct its hours.

The printed text reads τάχος, speed, while the apparatus records τὸ πάχος, thickness, at p. 286, lines 9–10. The model follows the edited text and its faster/slower comparison. Schöne relocates the twelve-finger conclusion into angle brackets and deletes its duplicate at the end. These are editorial decisions, not invisible repairs.

Line-end hyphens and whitespace are joined; apparatus, line numbers and deleted letters are omitted in the reading. The digital duplicate “μενον” after στοχασάμενον is removed following the page; ὀρῶν follows the printed mountain word. The full scans retain all editorial marks. The language notes distinguish interpretation from literal wording.

Collection is exact and complete in the model. Receiver shape, scale and centimetre dimensions are teaching choices. There is no pressure, friction, rainfall, leakage or instrument-error simulation. The chapter’s rain discussion motivates asking whether supply changes; it supplies no ten-second switching schedule.
